It’s pretty easy to pick up. In the style in RDO, you get two cards to start, then five more are played on the table. These are community cards that everyone uses, and the best five cards are your hand (if the best five are on the board, those are your five; if one of yours plus four on the table are best, that’s your hand; or your two plus three more).

The dealer rotates with each hand. The player to the dealer’s left is the “small blind.” They put in half the minimum bet by default. Next player is the “big blind.” They automatically bet the minimum bet. (These are $0.10 and $0.20 in the game.) This is designed to give more players an incentive to play.

Betting in the first hand starts with the next player, then the small-blind spot in subsequent rounds. You can either bet the minimum ($0.20), raise (up to the $5.00 max bet), or fold. If you raise, you’re signaling (in theory) that you have a good hand. Other players then have to match your bet to stay in that hand (if they also have a strong hand or think you’re bluffing) or can fold. 

After the first round of betting, three cards are played and it all starts over. The new addition is that you can “check,” which is essentially passing. If someone else bets, you have to match or fold. If no one bets because everyone checks, then play continues on to the next round. 

Third round, one more card is played. You now have six to choose from. Betting continues as before. 

A final round follows with a fifth card on the board. At the end of this round, it’s your best five vs. the best five of anyone else still in that hand. These best five are chosen automatically; you don’t have to actually know it. The game will let you know what you have. 

It gets *way* more complicated than that, but in a game with fake money where the players are mostly not great poker players, the complexity doesn’t matter nearly as much. If you really want to get into the details, you’ll know roughly what odds you have to get the cards you need, and you’ll have a good idea of what other players have based on how they bet. In RDO, though, that’s mostly irrelevant.

Minor point of contention, not on any selection, but on a description: 

> 50) Steve Kerr, 5x champion as a player, 3x as coach, Kerr was prolific shooter and **his three-point record stood uncontested** until being broken by the aforementioned, Kyle Korver

Although Kerr’s record was uncontested from the point of view of anyone breaking it, I’d contest it on the grounds that it was illegitimate to begin with. 

Kerr set the record in the 1994-95 season, when the NBA moved the line in from 23-9 to an even 22 feet. Three-point percentages rose across the NBA, and both Kerr and Tim Legler broke the previous record that season. 

The line moved back to the original 23-9 a few years later. 

I maintain that Jon Sundvold, the previous record holder at 52.2% in 1988-89, was the true owner of the record until Korver broke it in 2009-2010.

In NBA history, 50+% shooting from three has only been done eight times. Four of those eight times were in the three seasons the line was moved up. Sundvold was the first, and he held the record with a 23-9 line for more than two decades. (To be fair to Kerr, he did shoot 50.7% a year after Sundvold, so he’s one of the four people to hit at that rate with the real line; Korver and Kapono are the other two.)

This is perhaps the only time Sundvold will ever make any kind of NBA history/trivia thread. As a 6-2 shooting guard, he still played in nine NBA seasons, which is pretty damn impressive given he was a three-point specialist in an era that didn’t really appreciate threes. He retired a coupe years before the line moved up; if he were a few years younger and got to take advantage of that change, he might still own the record.
